summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Veritas through an Optimize-driven playbook that maps batching and KV (prefix) caching decisions to cost and latency outcomes. Customer cares about P95 latency under 350ms for core policy search flow, SOC2/compliance, and a 3-month pilot to validate unit economics.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-19 15:30 PT - duration ~52m. Attendees: Morgan (AE), Diego (SE), Priya (PM) from Redwood; Karen (CTO), Liam (Infra), Anita (ML), Ethan (Product) from Veritas.

[00:00] Morgan: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a 45-ish minute workshop runthrough of the Optimize playbook and then leave time for Q&A. i'm Morgan, account lead, and diego is our SE.
[00:18] Diego: hi all, quick outline: we'll map your traffic shape to batching settings, look at prefix/K-V caching (we sometimes see K-V written both ways) and then show the cost sim in the console. i also have a small sandbox we can run one or two p95 sims on if you want.
[00:34] Karen: great, we're mostly focused on the policy search microservice - it's a mix of short prompts (30-120 tokens) and some longer followups when underwriters augment content. must hit P95 <350ms for top 3 routes and keep data in our VPC.
[00:48] Morgan: noted. VPC + private options are definitely in scope. quick clarifying q: are you okay with a dedicated pool for the pilot or should we treat hosted first?
[00:58] Liam: security team prefers a private VPC but procurement won't sign for dedicated until we see clear cost savings vs hosted. so we'd like hosted pilot first then evaluate dedicated commit.
[01:10] Diego: fair. hosted + VPC-peering and then a dedicated decision after econ validation. we'll factor that into the simulation.

[01:25] Morgan: okay i'm going to share the console view -- link in chat: https://redwood.console/savings/veritas-demo (note: placeholder). you'll see the 'Optimize Playbook' tile.
[01:39] Anita: i shared the request histogram earlier but i'll resend the raw CSV after. it has spikes at 50 qps during business hours. most requests are 40-120 tokens.
[01:50] Diego: perfect, that's the shape i was hoping for. for that QPS range we typically see wins from two levers: batching (increasing tokens/second efficiency) and prefix/K-V caching for repeat prefixes like policy number + customer history.

[02:06] Diego: quick sketch — batching is continuous batching inside the runtime; the bigger your batch size the lower per-token overhead but higher latency for single requests. prefix cache returns tokens from the KV store so full generation is avoided for repeated starts. but cache hit rate depends on sessionization and how deterministic prompts are.
[02:28] Karen: can you quantify 'lower per-token'? like percent savings?
[02:33] Diego: in our console sim, for 50 qps with average 80-token requests, moving batch target from 1 to 4 yields ~22-28% token-cost reduction, assuming steady arrival. prefix cache at 30% effective hit rate can shave another 30% of generation cost because cached prefixes avoid a chunk of decoding. these numbers vary with distribution — but that's the ballpark.

[02:58] [03:00] Morgan: (interrupt) and the Optimize module will suggest batch size + cache TTLs based on your histograms; it also shows the expected P95 impact.
[03:12] Liam: what's the P95 tradeoff if we push batching? we can't compromise that 350ms target.
[03:18] Diego: good q. we did a rough sim using your P95 baseline and arrival jitter. with batch size 4 we saw median improve a bit, but P95 increased by ~70-90ms in the worst case if you have bursty, low concurrency users. that's because single requests wait to be accumulated. however with our smart routing you can set latency-first policy for top routes — those routes bypass batching or use a smaller max batch.
[03:44] Anita: how deterministic are prefixes for our use case? we often include dynamic fields like timestamp and session IDs which blow up cache effectiveness.
[03:53] Diego: exactly — you'll need to normalize prompts. two tactics: 1) template canonicalization (remove or hash dynamic tokens) before cache keying; 2) use sessionization so repeat multi-turn flows reuse KV caches. in our experiments, templating improved effective prefix hit by 18-25%.
[04:13] Ethan: is templating something Redwood does automatically or do we need code changes?
[04:18] Diego: small instrumentation change on your side — a preprocessor that normalizes prompts. we can provide examples. no large infra work.

[04:30] [04:30] Morgan: i'll drop the templating guide here: https://redwood.docs/prompt-normalization and the savings template spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/veritas-savings-template (these are demo links).
[04:45] Karen: thanks. what about cache TTLs? we have short-lived policy contexts and also long-lived templates. how do we choose TTLs?
[04:54] Diego: use two-tier TTLs: 1) short prefix TTL (a few seconds) for highly dynamic context; 2) longer TTL (minutes-hours) for static templates. our console suggests TTL buckets and simulates hit-rate by sampling your historical requests.
[05:10] Priya: also note Optimize will flag when cache keys are low entropy (too many unique keys) and recommend template extraction. it's part of the evaluation UI.

[05:22] [05:22] Liam: security, encryption on KV — do you encrypt at rest and can we plug-in our KMS?
[05:29] Diego: yes, KV storage supports encryption at rest and we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments. for hosted we have envelope encryption and can do BYOK for enterprise. we'll share the security appendix.

[05:40] Morgan: quick demo — switching to the console's cost sim: here we create two scenarios. Scenario A: conservative batching (target 2), no prefix cache. Scenario B: aggressive batching (target 4), prefix cache with 25% hit.
[05:58] [06:00] Diego: Scenario A cost projection $0.XXX per 1k tokens and p95 300ms. Scenario B shows $0.XXX-30% cost and p95 360-380ms in the worst-case. that delta is exactly where you decide per-route routing.
[06:18] Anita: can we set per-route policies? for example, underwriter route low latency, automated claims route cost-first?
[06:25] Morgan: yes per-route policies are first-class. you define routes in the console (by endpoint or API key) and attach policies: latency-first, cost-first, or balanced. you can also set canary percentages.

[06:37] [06:37] Ethan: curious about cold-starts with KV? I mean when cache misses happen do we pay full generation plus cache write overhead?
[06:46] Diego: yes you pay full generation on miss and the write cost (small) to populate the cache. but remember writes are often amortized across many subsequent hits. Optimize shows expected amortization break-even (requests-to-hit) based on your predicted hit curve.

[06:58] [07:00] Morgan: switching to a slightly different example: if you have session affinity and 20% of users are heavy repeaters, a session cache plus prefix caching can produce outsized savings because those users hit more often.
[07:12] Liam: can Redwood sessionize without cookies? we run microservices and have tokens passed around.
[07:17] Diego: yes sessionization can be keyed on user-id or device-id you send as metadata. we do not need cookies. it's just an additional key in the request metadata.

[07:28] [07:28] Karen: procurement will ask about multi-region — our infra spans east/us and eu-west. does the caching work cross-region or is it per-region?
[07:36] Priya: caches are per-region to keep latency predictable. you can replicate cache entries asynchronously for read locality, but that introduces replication cost and staleness tradeoffs. Optimize will simulate per-region cost.

[07:52] [08:00] Diego: here's a quick playback of the simulation using your 50 qps shape. i toggled template normalization on. when normalization is on, effective prefix hit jumps from ~12% to ~31% and cost drops about 21% in the model.
[08:15] Anita: wow that's meaningful. is normalization safe for regulatory logs and audit trails? we still need to preserve original user content for compliance.
[08:23] Diego: normalization is only for cache keys — you still retain the original prompt in your own logs. Redwood's console stores anonymized stats for the optimiser; raw prompts never get stored in our analytics unless you explicitly opt in. we'll include that on the security appendix.

[08:36] [08:40] Morgan: switching lanes: pilot design. for a 3-month pilot we recommend: week 1: telemetry and hist sampling + templating POC. week 2-3: sandbox perf runs + initial cache rules. month 1-2: run both hosted and dedicated cost sim; month 3: run production canary and final commit decision.
[08:58] Liam: how much work on our side for telemetry?
[09:03] Diego: about a couple engineers for a week to add metadata (route, user-id, template-id) to requests. we can supply a shim lib if you want.
[09:12] Karen: what's the rollback story if latency regresses after enabling caching/batching?
[09:17] Diego: rollbacks are via the console: change policy to latency-first or reduce allowed batch size; we also keep model variants for fallback to smaller models if needed. we have automatic fallbacks and can do canary rollouts by percent.

[09:30] [09:30] Morgan: competitor question — we often get asked why not just use a general-purpose edge cache or rely on the model provider's streaming.
[09:39] Priya: two points: edge caches don't know about model prefixes and decoding state, so they can't short-circuit autoregressive decoding the way prefix/KV cache does. and model-provider streaming doesn't address batching inefficiencies. our runtime interacts with model execution to save full decoding time on hits.
[09:58] Ethan: pricing model — is savings shown net of Redwood fees?
[10:03] Morgan: yes the console's projection shows net unit economics assuming typical Redwood hosted pricing (token + infra). for dedicated pools we provide separate committed pricing and the console will show that side-by-side.

[10:16] [10:16] Diego: demo pause — open Qs?
[10:20] Karen: compliance, do you support audit logs and external SIEM integration?
[10:24] Morgan: yes, we export audit logs to your S3/Cloud storage and can forward to Splunk or Datadog. SSO (SAML/Okta) and RBAC are supported.

[10:35] Anita: for the prompt normalization examples, can you share a small repo or snippet?
[10:39] Diego: i'll attach a snippet after the call. it's a tiny function (regex + hash for dynamic tokens).

[10:48] [10:50] Morgan: i'm going to capture a quick friction checklist: telemetry + sample CSV (customer), sandbox access (Redwood), templating POC, security docs.
[10:58] Liam: timeline: if we can get sandbox by next week and we provide CSV by Monday, we can do an initial perf run in two weeks. procurement might take 4-6 weeks after pilot.

[11:10] [11:10] Morgan: perfect. i'll summarize and send the next steps.
[11:14] Diego: final note: the Optimize console also has a scenario generator where you can adjust spike patterns and see breakpoints where batching harms p95. it's useful for SRE signoffs.
[11:26] Karen: good, i'd like to show this to our SRE and compliance leads.
[11:30] Morgan: action items and owners in chat. we'll also upload the savings spreadsheet pre-filled with current qps once we get your CSV.
[11:38] [11:38] Morgan: ok thanks everyone. we'll follow up with security docs and sandbox creds.

End of transcript.

Notes: a few transcribed terms may be fuzzy (K-V vs KV, template-normalization sometimes read as 'templating normalization'). References: security appendix link (to be emailed), demo console links (placeholders), savings spreadsheet placeholder.
